title: Protest of Environmental Law & Policy Center, Sierra Club, Citizens Action Coalition of Indiana, and Citizens Utility Board of Wisconsin re the 12/29/2025 Complaint against Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. under EL26-36.
entity: ENVIRONMENTAL LAW & POLICY CENTER; Sierra Club; Citizens Action Coalition of Indiana; Citizens Utility Board of Wisconsin

documents.name: EL26-36 PIOs Protest.docx
documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
BEFORE THE
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

PROTEST OF THE ENVIRONMENTAL LAW & POLICY CENTER,
SIERRA CLUB, CITIZENS ACTION COALITION OF INDIANA, 
AND CITIZENS UTILITY BOARD OF WISCONSIN

Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, the Environmental Law & Policy Center, Sierra Club, Citizens Action Coalition of Indiana, and the Citizens Utility Board of Wisconsin (“Public Interest Organizations” or “PIOs”) submit this response to the complaint of the Northern Indiana Public Service Company LLC (“NIPSCO”) against the Midcontinent Independent System Operator (“MISO”) filed with the Commission on December 29, 2025 (“Complaint”).
NIPSCO filed the Complaint in response to the December 23, 2025, Department of Energy Order No. 202-25-12 (“Order”) requiring the continued operation of two coal-fired units at the R.M. Schahfer power plant (“Schahfer” or “Schahfer Units”). The Order came just days before NIPSCO planned to retire the Schahfer Units pursuant to a settlement approved by the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission (“IURC”). The Order declared that “an emergency exists in portions of the Midwest region of the United States due to a shortage of electric energy, a shortage of facilities for the generation of electricity, and other causes.” and ordered NIPSCO and MISO to “take all measures necessary to ensure that Schahfer Units 17 and 18 are available to operate.” The Order further directed MISO to “take every step to employ economic dispatch of Schahfer Units 17 and 18 to minimize cost to ratepayers.”
As detailed below, PIOs oppose NIPSCO’s complaint, which contradicts the Order, fails to identify any beneficiaries of the Schahfer Units, and seeks compensation for an unlawful application of Section 202(c). The Commission should reject it.
INTRODUCTION
Schahfer Units 17 and 18 are outdated and unreliable coal-fired generators. Built in the 1980s, both units have experienced long and recurrent outages in recent years. They are expensive to maintain and operate. NIPSCO’s president himself recently admitted that for Unit 18 to continue operating, it “needs to be rebuilt,” which can take “6 months or longer.” Due to their high costs and lack of economic competitiveness, NIPSCO has planned and executed a decade-long process to replace these aging coal units with modern generation units. 
The Order overturned that process in the final hours, making it the latest in a line of orders requiring continued operation of soon-to-retire gas- or coal-fired units across the country. Since last spring, the Department of Energy has relied on Section 202(c) to prop up expensive plants across the country, overriding the resource planning decisions of states and nullifying the resource adequacy determinations of grid operators and state regulators. Far from identifying the sort of discrete emergency that Congress envisioned with the enactment of Section 202(c), the Department has repeatedly relied on vague claims of generalized “energy emergencies” to support its orders. The result is hundreds of millions of dollars in unnecessary costs. 
Like earlier orders, the Order misrepresents North American Electric Reliability Corporation planning documents and MISO residual capacity auction results to conclude a) that “an emergency exists in portions of the Midwest region of the United States due to a shortage of electric energy”;  and b) that these emergency conditions “will continue in the near term and are also likely to continue in subsequent years.” These determinations fly in the face of all available evidence—including evidence that the Order itself cites. Most telling is Department’s citation of a June 2025 Organization of MISO States survey, which found that MISO will have a “surplus of generation capacity” in 2026. That finding—which the Department quotes—undercuts the Department’s emergency declaration.
The Schahfer Order establishes more than two directives regarding NIPSCO’s and MISO’s operation of the plant: First, the Order says that “MISO is directed to take every step to employ economic dispatch of Schahfer Units 17 and 18 to minimize cost to ratepayers.” Second, the Order says that “[b]ecause this Order is predicated on the shortage of facilities for generation of electric energy and other causes, Schahfer Units 17 and 18 shall not be considered capacity resources.”
NIPSCO’s complaint relies on Section 202(c) to seek compensation for continued operation of the Schahfer Units. NIPSCO asks the Commission to allocate Schahfer’s costs across the MISO North and Central regions based on the “load ratio share” of the load-serving entities in those regions. NIPSCO states ”[c]urrently, there is no MISO Tariff provision that would permit NIPSCO’s costs of complying with the Department 202(c) Order to be allocated to LSEs in MISO’s northern and central zones” and that “[i]f left unaddressed, this would effectively prevent NIPSCO from recovering its costs via [Federal Power Act (“FPA”)] section 202(c).” NIPSCO does not seek a “determination of the actual costs that NIPSCO will recover,” instead stating that those costs “will be addressed in a future filing with the Commission.” NIPSCO does not provide any indication of the dollar amount of costs it will eventually seek to recover, and instead states that it intends to seek recovery for “all costs for the continued operation of Unit 17, and to return Unit 18 to operational status and its continued operation thereafter … net of market revenues.”
ARGUMENT
The Commission should reject NIPSCO’s complaint because ratepayers should not be subject to costs for unlawful 202(c) orders. The Commission should also reject NIPSCO’s complaint because NIPSCO’s proposed methodology cannot identify any benefits the Schahfer Units are providing to MISO North and Central customers that are not already compensated under existing provisions of the MISO tariff.  Absent such a showing, there is no case for NIPSCO to recover any costs beyond those already provided for in current tariff provisions. Furthermore, even if NIPSCO identified uncompensated benefits and who those benefits flowed to, it would still be improper, and in some cases would violate the filed-rate doctrine, to allow recovery of costs incurred prior to the issuance of Department’s 202(c) order or costs incurred for activities that go beyond what can be required by any 202(c) order.  
The Commission Should Not Require Ratepayers to Fund Unlawful 202(c) Orders.
 	NIPSCO asserts that it has a “statutory right to recover all of its Order Costs” and that “[t]his entitlement is established by the plain language of FPA Section 202(c), the Department Referral Regulation, and the Department 202(c) Order, itself.” NIPSCO does not allege any alternative need or legal basis for continuing to operate Schahfer and seeking  “to recover all costs associated with complying with the DOE 202(c) Order.” Thus, by the terms of NIPSCO’s complaint, the Commission’s authority to allocate costs to load-serving entities in MISO North and Central thus arises exclusively from the Order, which itself arises solely from Section 202(c).
The Commission should not allow NIPSCO to recover costs associated with the Order because it is unlawful. The Order addresses circumstances beyond the lawful scope of an emergency under Section 202(c) and fails to provide evidence or reasoned decision-making substantiating the existence of an emergency that can come within Section 202(c). The Order’s primary focus is long-term bulk-system reliability, which is not a basis to mandate generation under Section 202(c). Additionally, the Order does not, and could not, provide any valid evidence or reasoned decision-making to support its stated near-term resource adequacy concerns.
Separately, the Order suffers from other legal deficiencies. These include (1) the failure to exercise reasoned decision-making in imposing a requirement to “best meet” the claimed emergency and serve the public interest; (2) the imposition of availability requirements beyond the Department of Energy’s jurisdiction under Section 202(c); (3) the disallowance of capacity market treatment without reasoned decision-making and beyond jurisdictional limits; and (4) the failure to comply with limitations in section 202(c)(2), including failing to “ensure” that the Order requires generation only as needed to meet the claimed emergency and serve the public interest. 
Given the facially evident legal shortcomings with the Order, the Commission should, at a minimum, withhold any ruling on NIPSCO’s Complaint until legal challenges to the Order have been exhausted. As of this filing, the window for requesting rehearing on the Order remains open. Parties challenging the Order will, unless the Department grants rehearing, subsequently have the opportunity to seek review at the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals. Should any party do so, the Commission should allow the courts to determine whether the Order was lawful before approving a cost allocation methodology based on the Order. Even if the Commission determines that creating a cost allocation mechanism is appropriate, however, the Commission should, at a minimum, make clear that any and all costs assigned pursuant to the new tariff provision are subject to refund if the underlying 202(c) Order is found unlawful. 
Any Cost Recovery that the Commission Approves Must Adhere to the Cost Causation Principle. 
Most of the Commission’s electricity ratemaking takes place under the auspices of FPA Sections 205 or 206, which charge the Commission with ensuring “just and reasonable” rates and with rectifying “unjust and unreasonable” rates respectively. Courts have explained that this just and reasonable standard is the basis for foundational ratemaking principles, including the cost-causation principle, the rule against retroactive ratemaking, and the filed-rate doctrine. 
As the DC Circuit explains, the cost-causation principle requires that “in order to ensure just and reasonable rates, FERC must make some reasonable effort to match costs to benefits.” In Illinois Commerce Commission v. FERC, the 7th Circuit held that, “FERC is not authorized to approve a pricing scheme that requires a group of utilities to pay for facilities from which its members derive no benefits, or benefits that are trivial in relation to the costs sought to be shifted to its members.” The “cost-causation” and “beneficiary-pays” principles are two sides of the same coin, with courts and the Commission applying them interchangeably. They both make clear that, in order to set compensation that is just and reasonable, the Commission cannot allocate a facility’s costs to ratepayers who receive no material benefit from the facility.
While this ratemaking proceeding occurs under the auspices of a FPA Section 202(c)(1) rather than the more common FPA Sections 205 or 206, the statute similarly provides that “the Commission, after hearing held either before or after such order takes effect, may prescribe by supplemental order such terms as it finds to be just and reasonable, including the compensation or reimbursement which should be paid to or by any such party.” The just and reasonable standard mandated by the FPA applies in the 202(c) cost allocation context as well, and carries with it the bedrock “just and reasonable” derived ratemaking principles that the Commission considers in section 205 and 206 ratemaking cases.
NIPSCO takes issue with application of the filed-rate doctrine and prohibition against retroactive rulemaking—but it agrees that the cost-causation and beneficiary-pays principles should apply here. The Commission also recognized as much implicitly in the Campbell 202(c) cost allocation proceeding. There, the Commission correctly emphasized that the cost-causation principle is a relevant standard to apply in 202(c) recovery actions,  despite some parties arguing otherwise. Like in the Campbell 202(c) cost allocation order, the Commission must adhere to foundational ratemaking principles derived from the just and reasonable standard in any order it issues in this docket, including ensuring that any costs assigned are commensurate with the benefits.  
Application of Traditional Ratemaking Principles, Including the Beneficiary Pays Principle, Cannot Support NIPSCO’s Request for Broad Cost Recovery 
Applying these principles to the present circumstances reveals no basis for NIPSCO’s request for broad cost recovery on the costs NIPSCO incurs in purported compliance with the Order, for a few reasons. Generators in MISO are primarily compensated for capacity, energy, and operating reserves. As discussed further below, these payments are designed to provide compensation for generators at a just and reasonable rate for their contributions to the grid. The Schahfer Units cannot be compensated for any capacity contributions unless the Commission disregards the Order, because such a recovery would conflict with the Order’s directive that “Schahfer Units 17 and 18 shall not be considered capacity resources.” There is reason to believe that NIPSCO can receive compensation for the energy and ancillary services the Schahfer Units provide. Absent a showing that the current tariff provisions will not properly compensate NIPSCO for the energy and ancillary services the Schahfer Units provide to the grid, a new cost allocation tariff provision is unjustified.  And NIPSCO has not made that showing.  PIOs expound on each of these points in the following sections.
Schahfer cannot be compensated for providing capacity.
The Department order is clear: “Because this Order is predicated on the shortage of facilities for generation of electric energy and other causes, Schahfer Units 17 and 18 shall not be considered capacity resources.” Unless the Commission disregards the Order, the Commission cannot approve any compensation that arises from any capacity benefit from the Units. The Order did not say, for example, that the Units “cannot participate in the capacity market,” in which case they might still have provided capacity value outside of the market. Instead, the Department’s Order categorically prohibits the units from being considered capacity resources. And without the ability to recognize a corresponding benefit, it is not just and reasonable for the Commission to assign costs associated with Schahfer Unit capacity value to any MISO participants 
There are two additional reasons no capacity benefit should be realized: first, load-serving entities in MISO have already paid to acquire sufficient capacity for 2026, including a reserve margin, and will not benefit materially from any additional capacity Schahfer provides.  MISO’s 2025-2026 capacity auction procured sufficient generating supplies for both MISO as whole and Indiana specifically. The Schahfer Units did not participate in that auction, which means that their capacity is not required for MISO to maintain adequate supplies plus a reserve margin. The Order itself recognizes this reality, stating that MISO has a “small surplus of generation capacity in 2026” without the Schahfer Units. And second, the Schahfer Units wouldn’t even be capable of providing capacity if they were allowed to: as discussed in section D.ii below, the Schahfer Units require significant repairs which will likely take longer than the total length of the Order period before they can be reliably operated. Units that require such significant downtime are excluded from serving as capacity resources in MISO.
	NISPCO’s filing states that “the Department 202(c) Order… provide[s] for full cost recovery.” But the Order does no such thing. The Order is clear that “[r]ate recovery is available pursuant to 16 U.S.C. § 824a(c).” Traditional ratemaking principles require that costs be allocated commensurate with the benefits, and the Commission recognized the need to apply the principle that costs be allocated commensurate with benefits in 202(c) contexts in cost allocation proceedings for the Campbell plant. And as highlighted in the following section, MISO already has tariff provisions that allocate the costs associated with the Schahfer Units’ energy and ancillary services market participation. 
MISO will already adequately compensate Schahfer for providing energy and ancillary services. 
The Department 202(c) order directs MISO to employ economic dispatch of the Schahfer Units. And NIPSCO recognizes that it can collect market revenues in its filing. The cost allocation, and level of compensation, for market participation are already well defined in the MISO tariff, and already operate to reimburse market participants fully for any services they provide. On top of these standard energy market revenues, the MISO tariff is specifically designed to allow for extremely high compensation to generators during periods of scarcity—levels of compensation high enough that they meet or exceed the value of lost load. MISO has established (and the Commission approved) energy and operating reserve payments that play a critical role in ensuring resource adequacy in the region. In approving MISO’s resource adequacy construct, the Commission recognized that in MISO, more so than in other RTOs, “the ancillary services market, scarcity pricing and a long-term resource adequacy plan all play a role in ensuring resource adequacy.” Specifically, the Commission noted that MISO’s scarcity pricing diminished the “outstanding free-rider and investment incentive issues faced in other RTOs with tighter caps or lower scarcity pricing values.” Thus, even if costs associated with operating the Schahfer Units should be recoverable (which PIOs do not concede), existing mechanisms already allow for that recovery.
Nor could these existing cost-recovery mechanisms fairly be described as somehow insufficient.  This past April, the Commission approved tariff revisions that increased MISO’s Value of Lost Load (“VOLL”) to $10,000/MWh. This price is a cap and serves as an administratively set price during MISO-directed Energy Emergency Alert (EEA)-Level 3 load-shed events. The Commission found that MISO’s $10,000/MWh price “reasonably estimates the value residential loads place on avoiding load shedding.” As the Commission observed: 
“VOLL does guide investment and retirement decisions in the long term . . . [and] shortage price signals in the Day-Ahead and Real-Time markets, which are developed through the VOLL and [Operating Reserve Demand Curve], are also near-term signals to incent real-time actions by generation and demand resources during the Operating Day, or the day before the Operating Day, to avoid potential shortage conditions.” 

In short, in the extremely unlikely event that MISO actually uses the Schahfer Units’ specific energy production, or the even more unlikely event that this production helps MISO avoid or lessen the impact of a reliability event that “[led] to the loss of power to homes and businesses in the areas that may be affected by curtailments or power outages, presenting a risk to public health and safety,” the MISO tariff already contains provisions that would fully compensate NIPSCO for the value the Schahfer Units actually provide, at a rate that the Commission has determined is just and reasonable. Thus, in the absence of the Schahfer Units being enabled to provide capacity value, NIPSCO cannot demonstrate that MISO’s market will somehow fail to fully compensate them for any benefits the units provide.
NIPSCO must specifically articulate any uncompensated services it believes must be addressed per traditional ratemaking principles. 
To the extent NIPSCO feels additional recovery is necessary to ensure it is made whole for costs incurred in compliance with the Order, NIPSCO must demonstrate that such recovery meets the cost-causation principle.  The Commission would then also need to identity the benefits associated with a cost, and then determine to whom the benefits flow. Only then can the Commission determine who should be allocated costs. Providing such an analysis in the Commission’s order is a necessary prerequisite to the reasoned decision-making required by the FPA and Administrative Procedure Act. 
The Commission has said that a similar Department 202(c) order issued for the Campbell plant suggests that the scope of the emergency is in MISO zones 1-7. But even if the Commission must accept a Department order’s conclusion that 1) there is an emergency need, and 2) the order addresses that need, the Commission still must articulate what the benefits associated with the unit are in order to justify the relative level of benefits each of MISO zones 1-7 receive, and thus how to allocate costs among zones 1-7. The currently proposed load ratio share proposal suggests that the benefits are proportionally (or at least roughly proportionally) commensurate with load withdrawing from the MISO grid and in a manner that scales linearly with each average MW of electricity withdrawn. But NIPSCO does not justify that approach, and it is far from self-evident that benefits accrue in zone 1-7 in a way that is aligned roughly with load ratio share. NIPSCO must identify what the benefits are, not just who the beneficiaries are, in order for the Commission to make a reasoned determination that the costs are allocated among the beneficiaries in a manner that is roughly proportionate to the share of the benefits each beneficiary receives. 
Finally, in the event NIPSCO elects this path, the Commission should hold a hearing to discuss any such evidence.  Whether the simultaneity of cost-based compensation and market-based compensation causes duplicative recovery, whether any duplicative recovery renders the filed rate unjust and unreasonable, and the extent to which different MISO participants benefit from the Schahfer Units are genuine issues of material fact warranting a hearing, and in any event the Commission’s decision making would benefit from a broad variety of perspectives. 
The Commission Should Never Allow for Allocation of NIPSCO’s Non-Mandatory Compliance Costs Across MISO North
In its filing, NIPSCO’s request for a cost recovery mechanism suggests that recovery include NIPSCO’s costs for actions taken “before and during the Order Duration Period.” Costs incurred before the Order issued were not incurred in compliance with the Order or “in carrying out such order.” Additionally, the Department lacks authority under section 202(c) to mandate NIPSCO revive Schahfer Unit 18, and the Commission cannot allow recovery of imprudently incurred costs to revive Unit 18 in reliance on the Order.
Moreover, while PIOs maintain that the whole of NIPSCO’s cost allocation proposal is insufficiently supported, under no circumstances should the Commission approve a tariff that explicitly allows NIPSCO to recover costs that the Order did not explicitly mandate.  In particular, the Commission cannot allow NIPSCO to recover any costs incurred in advance of the Department’s Order, because allowing such recovery would a) violate the filed rate doctrine and rule against retrospective ratemaking; and b) create moral hazard by sanctioning generators incurring costs in anticipation of future 202(c) orders.  Similarly, NIPSCO should not be reimbursed for any actions taken in response to the Order that the Department does not have legal authority to mandate.
The Commission cannot allow recovery of costs incurred prior to the issuance of the Department’s Order.
“The filed-rate doctrine prohibits regulated entities from charging rates other than those properly filed with the appropriate federal regulatory authority, and permits those rates to be changed only prospectively.” Contrary to NIPSCO’s assertions, the caselaw is clear that the filed-rate doctrine, and its “corollary” the rule against retroactive ratemaking, are derived at least in part from the “just and reasonable” standard. Specifically, as the DC Circuit clarifies, they “play an important role in helping the Commission fulfill its statutory responsibility to ensure that regulated entities charge only rates that are just and reasonable”: Because recovery under FPA Section 202(c) requires compensation terms to be just and reasonable, the filed-rate doctrine and rule against retroactive ratemaking apply in this ratemaking context as well.
Until the Department issued the Order, the wholesale rate NIPSCO was entitled to earn for any operations of the Schahfer Units, and the parties responsible for those costs, were entirely controlled by the MISO tariff. If the Commission were to allow a new cost allocation methodology and, at some point in the future, new recovery of costs, for expenses incurred before the Department order was issued, NIPSCO would be impermissibly charging MISO ratepayers costs other than those in the relevant tariff on file with the Commission. In Landgraf v. USI Film Prods., the Supreme Court provided helpful guidance on retroactivity. The Court explained that a provision should be considered retroactive if “it would impair rights a party possessed when he acted, increase a party's liability for past conduct, or impose new duties with respect to transactions already completed.” NIPSCO conducted and completed countless transactions in MISO markets prior to the issuance of the Order premised on the market rules that NIPSCO would be paid a clearing price rather than cost-of-service. If NIPSCO were able to now recoup additional costs for plant operations during that period by dint of also being motivated by a 202(c) order it can claim it anticipated, it would change “duties with respect to transactions already completed” and retroactively charge a rate other than that which was on file with the Commission at the time of the transaction.
NIPSCO argues that the “reimbursement” language of FPA Section 202(c) allows for facilities under emergency orders from the Department to charge rates that are not on file with the Commission.  But this argument conflates pre-rate recovery with pre-order recovery.  While narrow exceptions may be made to allow for compliance with emergency directives before new corresponding rate structures have been put into place, nothing in FPA Section 202(c) suggests that expenses incurred prior to the issuance of the 202(c) order itself should be included in the FPA’s few “‘narrow exception[s]’ to the . . . general prohibition on retroactive rate modification.”
Allowing NIPSCO to recover costs incurred in anticipation of a 202(c) order would also create moral hazard. A precedent that allows generators to incur expenses and receive cost recovery on those expenses by courting a 202(c) order will allow generators to shift costs on to other ratepayers, encourage inefficient investment decisions, and undermine confidence in market pricing signals. 
The Commission Must State that NIPSCO Cannot Recover Costs Imprudently Incurred, Including Costs to Revive Schahfer Unit 18.
Schahfer Unit 18 is broken and requires significant expenditures to be revived. As NIPSCO’s president explained recently before the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission:
“Unit 18 is in a forced outage; that one will take more time and effort for it to ultimately get it to where it needs to be, and at some point, if we do get a 202(c) [order], and it continues, we’ll likely have to do some work on [Unit] 17 as well. […] We’ve taken some steps to be prepared – long lead time equipment, in particular, that ultimately would have to be ordered for us to come in. Frankly, that unit needs to be rebuilt. […] We’re taking some steps to be able to do that, but it will take time; it can take 6 months or longer for us to ultimately be able to get that unit back to where it would need to be to operate for an extended period of time. It’s just the reality of that unit being close to retirement. We’re not completely unprepared, but it will take time to get that long lead time items in to be able to make the repairs necessary.”

The Department does not have authority under section 202(c) to mandate NIPSCO revive a generation facility, including Schahfer Unit 18. NIPSCO is on notice of this limitation.
The prudence standard applies to the question of whether costs allegedly incurred pursuant to a 202(c) order may be recovered. 
It would be imprudent for NIPSCO to expend money to revive Schahfer Unit 18 without, at minimum, carefully evaluating the legality of the Department’s Order, particularly any element of the Order that could be interpreted to direct repair of Unit 18 to an operational condition. The overwhelming weight of authority establishes that the Department has no authority to revive Schahfer Unit 18. Thus, it would be imprudent for NIPSCO to commit to major expenditures at the Unit based on an overly expansive (and illegal) interpretation of the Order; the Commission should make clear in its Order that, regardless of its overall decision on a cost allocation methodology, no imprudent expenditures can ever be reimbursed.
NIPSCO should not be able to seek reimbursement for expenditures associated with Unit 18, because it cannot provide any value during the period of this order
Separately and apart from PIOs’ prudency concerns above, the Commission should disallow any recover for Unit 18 for the additional reason that it cannot provide any benefit to MISO ratepayers.  Unit 18 is broken and evidently cannot provide any benefits to MISO customers and cannot address any emergency identified by the Department’s Order. As such, there is no possible basis for allocation of costs associated with the unit to MISO ratepayers.





CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, PIOs respectfully request that the Commission reject NIPSCO’s complaint.

Respectfully submitted,						Dated: January 20, 2026

Attachment A
 December 30, 2025

Erin Whitehead
Vice President, Regulatory Policy and Major Accounts
Northern Indiana Public Service Company LLC
801 E. 86th Ave.
Merrillville, IN 46410
317-965-8334
ewhitehead@nisource.com

Re: DOE Order No. 202-25-12 to Schahfer Units 17 and 18

Dear Ms. Whitehead:

   We represent Citizens Action Coalition of Indiana, Just Transition Northwest
Indiana, Hoosier Environmental Council, and Sierra Club in connection with this
matter. As you know, on December 23, 2025, the U.S. Department of Energy (“DOE”
or the “Department”) issued Order No. 202-25-12 (the “Order”). Northern Indiana
Public Service Company LLC (“NIPSCO”) might expend money due to the Order.
Such expenditures are recoverable from ratepayers only if prudent.

   We write to emphasize the following points: NIPSCO must carefully evaluate
whether it would be prudent to expend money to repair R.M. Schahfer
Generating Station (“Schahfer”) Unit 18 due to the Order. There are several
legal bases to conclude that DOE lacks authority under section 202(c) to
direct NIPSCO to revive the generation facility. We intend to litigate the
recovery of any imprudently incurred expenditures. Those points are further
explained below.

   A. Schahfer Unit 18 Is Broken and Cannot Operate Without Substantial
      Expenditures.

    The Order (at page 5) purports to direct NIPSCO to “take all measures necessary
to ensure that Schahfer Units 17 and 18 are available to operate.” In the case of Unit
18, these measures may be extensive. As you know, Schahfer Unit 18 experienced a
forced outage of 2,980 hours from February 16, 2025 to June 23, 2025 due to the L-1
 turbine blade separating from its root.1 On July 9, 2025, Schahfer experienced
another forced outage lasting 1,996 hours (nearly three months) due to significant
damage to the upper portion of the condenser tubes including separation of a portion
of one L-0 blade.2

    NIPSCO’s President, Mr. Vincent Parisi, stated at the recent 2025 Winter
Reliability Forum before the IURC – predating the recent Order – that “Unit 18 is in
a forced outage; that one will take more time and effort for it to ultimately get it to
where it needs to be, and at some point, if we do get a 202(c) [order], and it continues,
we’ll likely have to do some work on [Unit] 17 as well. […] We’ve taken some steps to
be prepared – long lead time equipment, in particular, that ultimately would have to
be ordered for us to come in. Frankly, that unit needs to be rebuilt. […] We’re taking
some steps to be able to do that, but it will take time; it can take 6 months or longer
for us to ultimately be able to get that unit back to where it would need to be to
operate for an extended period of time. It’s just the reality of that unit being close to
retirement. We’re not completely unprepared, but it will take time to get that long
lead time items in to be able to make the repairs necessary.”3

   We expect that the expenditure to procure and install the referenced long lead
time equipment to revive Unit 18 – instead of allowing the units to retire as
previously planned – will be substantial. Before incurring any of those costs, NIPSCO
must carefully evaluate whether the expenditure is prudent.

    B. DOE Lacks Authority Under Section 202(c) to Direct NIPSCO to Revive
       Schahfer Unit 18.

    In directing NIPSCO and MISO to “take all measures necessary to ensure”
Schahfer Unit 18 is “available to operate,” and directing MISO “to take every step to
employ economic dispatch” of Schahfer Unit 18, Order at 5, the Department exceeded
its authority under Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act and impermissibly
intruded on the authority over generating facilities that Section 201(b) of the statute
reserves to Indiana, 16 U.S.C. §§ 824(b)(1), 824a(c)(1). The sweeping language in the
Order would encompass physical and all other changes necessary to revive Schahfer
Unit 18, a generation facility that is in disrepair and that, until just seven days ago,
was undergoing closure. The Federal Power Act’s language, structure, legislative
history, and interpretation by the courts all confirm that the Department’s Order is
unlawful.


1 Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission (“IURC”) Cause No. 38706 FAC 148, NIPSCO Exhibit 4,

Direct Testimony of David Saffran (Aug. 18, 2025), Att. 4-A, at 1.
2 IURC Cause No. 38706 FAC 149, NIPSCO Exhibit 4, Direct Testimony of David Saffran (Nov. 20,

2025), Att. 4-A, at 2.
3 IURC 2025 Winter Reliability Forum (December 2, 2025), video recording available at
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bCzALF4V45M, at 51:35 and 52:48 timestamps.


                                                  2
     The structure and language of the Federal Power Act reflect Congress’s deliberate
choices to preserve the states’ traditional authority over generating facilities and to
circumscribe the Department’s emergency authority in light of the states’ role. The
first sentence of the Federal Power Act declares that federal regulation extends “only
to those matters which are not subject to regulation by the States.” Id. § 824(a).
Section 201(b)(1) states that, except as otherwise “specifically” provided, federal
jurisdiction does not attach to “facilities used for the generation of electric energy.”
Id. § 824(b)(1). The courts have held that Section 201(b)(1) reserves to the states
authority over electric generating facilities, see, e.g., Hughes v. Talen Energy Mktg.,
LLC, 578 U.S. 150, 155 (2016), including the authority to order their closure, Conn.
Dep’t of Pub. Util. Control v. FERC, 569 F.3d 477, 481 (D.C. Cir. 2009) (explaining
that under Section 201(b), states retain the right “to require the retirement of
existing generators” or to take any other action in their “role as regulators of
generation facilities”). Congress also recognized the states’ exclusive authority over
generating facilities in Section 202(b), which provides that the Federal Energy
Regulatory Commission’s interconnection authority does not include the power to
“compel the enlargement of generating facilities for such purposes.” 16 U.S.C.
§ 824a(b).

   There is a clear distinction between authority to regulate generation facilities and
the Department’s authority under Section 202(c) to require generation of electric
energy. Electric energy is an electromagnetic wave, and its “generation, delivery,
interchange, and transmission” is the creation and propagation of that wave. See
Brief Amicus Curiae of Electrical Engineers, Energy Economists and Physicists in
Support of Respondents at 2, New York v. FERC, 535 U.S. 1 (2002); see also Edison
Electric Institute Glossary of Electric Utility Terms (1991 ed.) (defining electric
generation as “the act or process of transforming other forms of energy into electric
energy”). Section 202(c)(1), like the rest of the Federal Power Act, is written “in the
technical language of the electric art” and federal jurisdiction generally “follow[s] the
flow of electric energy, an engineering and scientific, rather than a legalistic or
governmental test.” Conn. Light & Power v. Fed. Power Comm’n, 324 U.S. 515, 529
(1945); see also Fed. Power Comm’n v. Fla. Power & Light Co., 404 U.S. 453, 454, 467
(1972).

    The scope of the Department’s emergency power under Section 202(c) is bounded
both by the provision’s specific language and Congress’s clear intention and repeated
direction in the Federal Power Act to respect the states’ authority over generating
facilities. When an actual emergency exists, Section 202(c)(1) authorizes the
Department to require just two specific things: (1) “temporary connections of
facilities” and (2) “generation, delivery, interchange, or transmission of electric
energy.” Id. § 824a(c)(1). The only reference to “facilities” in the authorizing provision
of Section 202(c)(1) appears in the clause relating to temporary connections, not in
the clause pertaining to “generation” of electric energy. And that clause only
authorizes connections “of” facilities; it does not provide authority to regulate the
facilities. The differences in Congress’s word choice in these clauses—referencing


                                            3
 “facilities” in one authorizing provision but not the other—must be given effect. See,
e.g., Gallardo v. Marstiller, 596 U.S. 420, 430 (2022); Gomez-Perez v. Potter, 553 U.S.
474, 486 (2008).

    Given Congress’s use of the term “generating facilities” elsewhere in the statute,
if it had intended to give the Department authority over generating facilities in
Section 202(c)(1), it would have done so explicitly. Instead, the provision
conspicuously excludes authority to manage the physical characteristics of power
plants. Congress purposely limited and particularized the Department’s emergency
powers, carefully avoiding intrusion on the states’ authority over generating facilities
recognized in Section 201(b)(1). See S. Rep. No. 74-621, at 19 (1935) (explaining that
the emergency powers in Section 202(c)(1) “which were indefinite in the original bill
have been spelled out with particularity”); compare S. 1725, Cong. Tit. II § 203(a)
(providing in original, unenacted bill that control of the production and transmission
of electric energy “except in time of war or other emergency declared to exist by
proclamation of the President, shall, as far as practicable, be by voluntary
coordination”), with 16 U.S.C. § 824a(c)(1) (providing particularized, specific
authorities and circumstances in which the authorities may be exercised).

    Under certain conditions, the Department may require generation of electric
power, and a utility may properly take steps at the facility to produce the power. It is
commonplace in the electric sector for the federal regulator properly acting within its
authority to cause effects in a state regulator’s jurisdictional sphere, and vice versa.
See Fed. Energy Regul. Comm’n v. Elec. Power Supply Ass’n, 577 U.S. 260, 281 (2016).
But the federal regulator may neither directly regulate generation facilities nor
impose requirements aimed at the facilities, even if nominally regulating within its
sphere. See id. at 281–82; see also Hughes, 578 U.S. at 164–65. Such encroachment is
impermissible, even in a real emergency or in a wrongly claimed one. See Conn. Light
& Power, 324 U.S. at 530 (“Congress is acutely aware of the existence and vitality of
these state governments. It sometimes is moved to respect state rights and local
institutions even when some degree of efficiency of a federal plan is thereby
sacrificed.”). Thus, the Department may not require generation that necessitates the
utility taking steps reserved to state authority, such as building a new generating
unit or refurbishing a broken one.

   As such, Congress did not give the Department sweeping authority to order
NIPSCO and MISO to revive Schahfer Unit 18. The directive to “take all measures
necessary to ensure” Schahfer Unit 18 is “available to operate” includes repairs or
modifications to physical facilities and other measures going far beyond electric
power generation. Because the plant is at the end of its useful life, with years of
forgone maintenance and capital expenditures, and in a state of disrepair, the
Department’s Order essentially requires rebuilding significant parts of the plant.
Nowhere does the statute empower the Department to issue such directive, and the
Department’s Order is facially ultra vires. The Order also contravenes Congress’s



                                           4
 repeated direction in the Federal Power Act to respect the states’ authority over
generating facilities.

   C. FERC’s Prudence Requirement Does Not Allow NIPSCO to Recover Costs
      Expended Pursuant to an Unlawful Directive.

   The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) holds authority to provide
for compensation or reimbursement of the costs of operation pursuant to a
Department order under section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act. 16 U.S.C.
§ 824a(c)(1); see also Consumers Energy Co. v. Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Op., Inc., 193
FERC ¶ 61,228, at P 31 (2025). The prudence standard applies to the question of
whether costs allegedly incurred pursuant to a 202(c) order may be recovered.
Consumers Energy Co. v. Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Op., Inc., 192 FERC ¶ 61,158, at
P 42 (2025). Specifically, in ruling on a proposed cost allocation for Section 202(c)
costs incurred by Consumers Energy Company, FERC explains:

      While this order approves the cost allocation methodology in the
      Proposed Tariff Provision, it does not approve recovery of actual costs.
      Pursuant to the Proposed Tariff Provision, Consumers must petition the
      Commission in a separate proceeding at a later date for approval to
      recover specific DOE Order Costs before ratepayers can be charged for
      such costs. Parties may raise issues related to the scope of costs prudently
      incurred pursuant to the DOE Order in that proceeding. Parties also may
      take appropriate steps, such as requesting rehearing in this proceeding,
      to preserve arguments that if the DOE Order were to be modified, then
      the Commission should require refunds or otherwise revisit its approach
      to matters that DOE referred to the Commission in connection with the
      DOE Order.

Id. (emphasis added and footnote omitted).

    Under its prudence standard, FERC must determine whether costs incurred by a
utility “are costs which a reasonable utility management . . . would have made, in
good faith, under the same circumstances, and at the relevant point in time.” Violet
v. FERC, 800 F.2d 280, 282–83 (1st Cir. 1986) (quoting New Eng. Power Co., 31 FERC
¶ 61,047, 61,084 (1985)); see La. Pub. Serv. Comm’n, 181 FERC ¶ 61,135, at P 177
(2022) (“The Commission’s prudence review standard is as follows: To determine the
prudence of an investment, the Commission evaluates whether a reasonable utility
manager would have made the same investment under the same circumstances. A
prudence inquiry addresses whether the utility conducted reasonable evaluation of
the costs and benefits prior to incurring a financial commitment. A prudence
determination is based upon what the utility knew or should have known at the time
a decision was made. The prudence standard ensures that ratepayers are not
required to pay for unnecessary costs.” (cleaned up)). Moreover, “where some other
participant in the proceeding creates a serious doubt as to the prudence of an


                                           5
 expenditure, then the applicant has the burden of dispelling these doubts and proving
the questioned expenditure to have been prudent.” Minnesota Power & Light Co.
(Opinion No. 86), 11 FERC ¶ 61,312, 61,644-45 (1980). FERC’s prudence standard
establishes that “[t]he Commission will not disallow costs as imprudent if they are
costs ‘which a reasonable utility management . . . would have made, in good faith
under the same circumstances, and at the relevant point in time.’” Columbia Gas
Transmission, LLC, 158 FERC ¶ 61,092, at P 8 (2017) (quoting New England Power
Co., 31 FERC ¶ 61,047, at 61,084 (1985)).

   A utility’s prudence determination necessarily includes a judgment as to the
legality of some regulatory treatment that affects costs. “We agree with the FPC
[Federal Power Commission] that at the time of the spin-off to the affiliate [the
subject gas pipeline company] was, or should have been, aware that gas purchased
from the affiliate might be priced [via Commission order] on the basis of cost of
service.” Cities Gas Service Co. v. Federal Power Commission, 424 F.2d 411, 417 (10th
Cir. 1969) (affirming FPC’s reduction of company’s jurisdictional gas pipeline rates).

    Yesterday, NIPSCO stated in a filing that NIPSCO has “begun planning related
to ongoing operations and maintenance and capital investments, including
investments that will be needed to bring Unit 18 back into operation following an
extended outage.” Complaint of N. Ind. Pub. Serv. Co. LLC, FERC Docket No. EL26-
36-000, at 10 (Dec. 29, 2025), FERC Accession No. 20251229-5444. In addition,
NIPSCO states that it engaged in discussions with DOE in anticipation of the Order.
Id.

   It would be imprudent for NIPSCO to expend money to revive Schahfer Unit 18
without, at minimum, carefully evaluating the legality of the Department’s Order,
particularly any element of the Order that could be interpreted to direct repair of
Unit 18 to an operational condition. As discussed above, the overwhelming weight of
authority establishes that the Department’s directive to revive Schahfer Unit 18 is
unlawful. A reasonable utility management does not in good faith expend money in
response to an unlawful directive, particularly when the utility management is on
notice of the unlawful nature of the directive. Additionally, under Indiana’s Federally
Mandated Costs law, any costs approved for recovery must be just and reasonable.
I.C. § 8-1-8.4-4(b). And expenditures that are unnecessary, excessive, or imprudent,
as well as expenditures that are not used and useful for ratepayers, may not be
recoverable. I.C. § 8-1-2-48(a); NIPSCO Ind. Grp. v. N. Ind. Pub. Serv. Co., 100 N.E.3d
234, 238 (Ind. 2018); Citizens Action Coalition of Indiana v. NIPSCO, 485 N.E.2d 610,
613-615 (Ind. 1985).

    In response to the Department’s Order, you recognize “the importance of both
reliability and cost management for [y]our customers” and commit to “continue to
engage with federal, state and local stakeholders as [you] adapt to evolving regulatory
requirements.” NIPSCO, Federal Order Delays NIPSCO’s R.M. Schahfer Generating
Station’s Retirement (Dec. 24, 2025), https://www.nipsco.com/our-company/news-


                                          6
 room/news-article/federal-order-delays-nipsco-s-r.m.-schahfer-generating-station-s-
retirement. Your recognition and commitment underscore your obligation to not
imprudently expend money to revive Schahfer Unit 18 in response to DOE’s unlawful
directive, notwithstanding your indication that you “are reviewing the overall impact
to [y]our customers and company and will comply with this order, and any subsequent
orders, if received.” Id. In a recent Section 202(c) matter involving Consumers Energy
Company (“CEC”) and its J.H. Campbell Generating Plant, CEC submitted a request
to the Department for clarification on the scope of authorization in the Department’s
August 20, 2025 order.4 This approach is within NIPSCO’s options in the instant
matter as part of an appropriate evaluation of a prudent course of action. NIPSCO
could also seek clarification from a court of competent jurisdiction to pronounce on
the legality of the Order.
